SEC15A-01.convention: 'one of the few X that is' with notional singular agreement is widely attested and accepted by several usage authorities (Merriam-Webster, Garner notes it as common); strict prescriptive grammar takes the plural antecedent 'components'
SEC15A-01.note: Relative 'that' takes plural 'components', and present tense ('now cut', 'may spend') rules out C/D. A is attractive because 'The balance spring ... is one of' primes singular, and the 'one of those that' construction is a contested usage point the real SAT generally avoids testing.
SEC15A-01.drop_reason: Not exclusive: 'one of the few components that is shaped' (A) is a widely accepted notional-singular usage that major usage guides do not condemn; the key rests on a contested prescriptive rule the real SAT avoids testing. The explanation is coherent only under the strict reading.

SEC15A-02.note: 'for many generations by the time ... arrived in 1896' demands the past perfect (progressive) for an action continuing up to a past point. A (present perfect) is the strongest lure for readers keying on 'for many generations'; C's future is struck on narrative tense.

SEC15A-03.note: 'together with' introduces a parenthetical, not a compound subject, so the head 'core' takes singular 'indicates'; the 'that'-clause object rules out the passives C/D. B is the strong lure (looks compound; nearest nouns 'huts'/'samples' plural).

SEC15A-04.note: The infinitive phrase 'To reconstruct ... priests' is the subject and needs a finite singular verb; A/B leave the sentence with no main verb. C is attractive via attraction to 'farmers, innkeepers, and village priests' and because the long infinitive can be misread as a purpose phrase awaiting a subject.

SEC15A-05.note: Singular possessive for 'tunnel' (or mountain): 'its'. C and D are contraction/possessive confusions rejectable in isolation; only A ('their', luring toward 'seeds' or 'slopes') requires tracking the antecedent.

SEC15A-06.note: 'both recorded ... and copied' is a correlative compound predicate; no punctuation separates the two verb phrases. B is attractive because the first conjunct is long and contains a list, inviting a comma before 'and'.

SEC15A-07.note: 'an island whose ...' is a nonrestrictive appositive renaming Murano at sentence end, set off by a comma. Semicolon and period leave a fragment ('an island whose ... secret'); A abuts two noun phrases, a pattern that is essentially never right.

SEC15B-01.note: Plural head 'escapements' plus 'since the first sea trials in 1774' requires plural present perfect. C is the strong lure via attraction to 'prototype' and the singular-sounding 'its drawings'; B is right on number but wrong on tense.

SEC15B-02.note: Rags are acted on ('by itinerant peddlers') in the 1340s: past passive. C ('collected') is the lure because it can be misread as a past participle completing the subject, leaving no main verb, or as active voice with rags as collectors.

SEC15B-03.note: A completed action dated 'in the spring of 1857' takes simple past. All options are singular, so the long appositive with 'posts' tests nothing; B (present perfect with a specific past date) is the only plausible lure.

SEC15B-04.note: Singular subject 'silkworm', separated by a long appositive, needs a finite singular verb; B/C leave no main verb. A lures via attraction to 'farmers' and 'groves'.

SEC15B-05.note: The first sentence is a statement containing an indirect question ('puzzled over how ...'), so it ends with a period; the next clause is independent. A (question mark) is the classic lure; C is a comma splice, D a fused sentence.

SEC15B-06.note: 'its bronze ... proving too brittle' is a nominative absolute (participle, no finite verb), attached with a comma. B and C are strong lures because 'its bronze' looks like the start of a new independent clause until one finds that 'proving' is not finite; D runs the absolute into the prepositional phrase.

SEC15B-07.note: 'Only the households drawing water ...' is a restrictive participial modifier (it identifies which households) and the subject continues to 'escaped', so no punctuation. A (comma) is attractive but would need a closing comma before 'escaped' and would make the modifier nonrestrictive, contradicting 'Only'; B/D separate subject from its own restrictive modifier.

tells: In the five punctuation/boundary items (A-06, A-07, B-05, B-06, B-07) the semicolon option, the colon option and the dash option are never the key; a test-taker who always strikes ';', ':' and the em dash loses nothing. Keys are no-mark (A-06, B-07), comma (A-07, B-06) or period (B-05).

Long-intervening-modifier SVA items lean singular: A-03, A-04, B-04 all key the singular verb against a nearby plural noun (huts/priests/farmers). 'Pick the singular when a plural noun sits next to the blank' scores 3 of 5 agreement items; A-01 and B-01 (plural keys) are the only counterweights.

In the three items whose options vary tense only (A-02, B-02, B-03) the key is the one consistent with the explicit past date in the sentence (1896, 1340s, 1857); the date is always printed, so 'match the date' solves each without the subject.
A-05 has two options struck in isolation (it's/they're), making it a two-way item.

phase2_note: All 14 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses) and every explanation's reasoning produces its key and rejects each distractor. One drop recommended: A-01 (one-of-the-few-that agreement is contested; A is defensible). Not drops but weak for a module-2 hard route: A-05 (two options struck in isolation), A-07 and B-03 (easy, one live distractor). Batch-level tells from phase 1 stand and are confirmed by the keys: semicolon/colon/dash never keyed across the 5 punctuation items; 3 of 5 long-modifier SVA items key the singular; tense-only items are solved by matching the printed date.
